newsitem.title: FRANCE: Investors seek news on Axa-UAP "deal of century".
newsitem.headline: Investors seek news on Axa-UAP "deal of century".

text.p: Investors are hoping for a progress report on the megamerger of French insurers Axa and UAP when their 1996 results are announced on Wednesday.

Axa and Union des Assurances de Paris (UAP) are integrating their operations after surprising financial markets last November by announcing they would combine operations to form the world's second largest insurer in terms of premium income.

Analysts expect robust 1996 operating earnings for Axa and formerly state-owned UAP. But provisions to prevent UAP's money-losing operations weighing on the new group are expected to plunge UAP into a big bottom line loss.
It will be the last time the two companies, France's largest insurers, release separate sets of figures. As of this year, their accounts will be consolidated.

Axa, which has grown from a sleepy mutual into a global player in two decades, called the 40 billion franc ($7 billion) stock swap the "deal of the century" and insisted it was an "operation between equals". But with Axa dominating the new group's executive lineup, it has become clear UAP has taken a back seat.

Axa, which has enjoyed a reputation as the best quality play in the French sector, has already said it is "at ease" with analysts' forecasts of 1996 net attributable profit of 3.6.-3.9 billion francs, up from 1995 profit of 2.73 billion.
This would represent earnings per share growth of 18 to 28 percent. But some analysts say Axa could surprise with profits of four billion francs or slightly higher.
The performance will be helped by strong results from Australian life insurer National Mutual and The Equitable of the United States, two of its biggest acquisitions this decade.

But UAP's accounts are expected to undergo a "once and for all" clean-up, pushing it into loss for second year in a row. Press reports say UAP whose state-owned past is viewed as having made it more stodgy and bureaucratic than Axa, will post a six-to-seven billion franc 1996 loss after provisions.

"A purge of UAP's acounts which would be translated by a loss of six billions would be...appreciated by the market," said analyst Jean-Baptiste Bellon of Deutsche Bank. UAP had a 1995 loss of 2.1 billion after heavy property provisions.
The new provisions are expected to be used to tackle restructuring, insurance and banking problems and analysts say they could knock six percent off UAP's net asset value.
But analysts are looking for operating earnings for UAP of 1.71 billion francs in 1996, helped by strong non-life results, particularly in France and Germany.

But uppermost in analysts' minds will be questions about how the merger is going. When talk first surfaced of a marriage between Axa and UAP, analysts dismissed it saying they were incompatible because of their overlapping French and British operations and different corporate cultures.
Axa has said the merger should allow 1997 savings of about 200 million francs and analysts say the best-case scenario calls for costs savings of 2.1 billion francs by 1999.

Some analysts say if anyone is capable of squeezing value out of UAP, Axa, with its shareholder-oriented philosophy, should be able to. But others are not convinced the merger will meaningfully improve Axa's earnings profile. In the past, Axa's chief attraction was its diversification overseas and lack of exposure to the French market. With UAP, that will change.

"The 'old Axa' was more plugged into exciting high-growth operations," said Brian Shea of Salomon Brothers, noting the weighting of the group's premium income generated by its most "exciting franchises", The Equitable and National Mutual, will fall by more than half to 15 percent from 32 percent.
